query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of Y (e.g., 1 at.%) to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy can improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance without sacrificing its mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of Y (e.g., 1 at.%)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, as the records judged to transfer do not provide a clear mechanism for the target system
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxidation resistance and maintained mechanical performance
generation.boundary: Temperature: 1000 °C, atmosphere: oxidizing, exposure time: several hours, mechanical loading: tensile loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Y to be added and the optimal processing route are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and oxidation resistance testing of the Y-added HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-added HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy shows decreased mechanical performance or poor oxidation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified
